items.stem: Which statement about how humans use the Earth's resources is correct?

options.text: Earth's resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport
Earth's resources means the fuels and metals dug from rock
Farmed crops count as synthetic and not as resources
Earth's resources supply transport but not warmth

items.why: The specification states exactly this use of the Earth's resources.

items.stem: Natural resources are supplemented by agriculture. Which list of products does the specification give for these resources?

options.text: Warmth, shelter, transport and heavy machinery
Food, timber, clothing and fuels are all provided
Food and clothing only, since fuels are all synthetic
Only timber and other farmed plant materials

items.why: The specification states that natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

items.stem: Which pair correctly matches a natural product with the synthetic product that can replace it?

options.text: Natural cotton fibre is replaced by farmed wool fibre
Natural rubber from latex is replaced by iron and steel
Natural rubber from latex replaced by synthetic rubber
Farmed timber is replaced by synthetic wood made from trees

items.why: Latex tapped from rubber trees is a natural product and synthetic rubber, made industrially, supplements and replaces it.

items.stem: Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed. What does the specification say this provides?

options.text: Renewable supplies that will never be used up
Only fuels and metals dug straight out of the rock
Metal ores that are then recycled indefinitely by us
Energy and the materials that people can use

items.why: The specification states that finite resources are processed to provide energy and materials.

items.stem: What makes a resource finite rather than renewable?

options.text: It cannot be recycled after it has been used
It is used up more quickly than it is replaced
It is buried underground rather than grown
It cannot be used more than a single time

items.why: A finite resource is not being replaced, or is replaced far more slowly than it is used, so it will run out.

items.stem: A student is given data on four materials. Which one should be classified as a renewable resource?

options.text: Copper ore, because copper can be melted and reused
Crude oil, because more is still being discovered
Timber, because the trees felled are all replanted
Natural gas, as it forms constantly underground

items.why: Trees are replaced at a rate that keeps pace with use, so timber is renewable.

items.stem: Which of these best describes sustainable development?

options.text: Development that uses none of the natural resources of the Earth at all
Development that meets the needs of future generations rather than those of people now
Development in which every material that industry uses is recycled afterwards
Development that meets the needs of today without compromising future ones

items.why: This is the definition given in the specification.

items.stem: What role does the specification say chemistry plays in the use of the Earth's resources?

options.text: It improves agricultural and industrial processes
It replaces farming entirely with synthetic factory products
It removes the need to use finite resources at all
It is only useful once a resource has already run out

items.why: The specification says chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and contributes to sustainable development.

items.stem: A table shows the volume of water used per person per day in four countries. Which conclusion can be drawn from the table alone?

options.text: The country with the largest figure uses the largest total volume
The country using the least water per person has the driest climate
The country with the largest figure uses more per person than the others
Water use per person is going to keep rising in every country

items.why: This is the only claim supported by a table of volume per person per day.

items.stem: A river sample contains 12 mg/dm3 of dissolved solids; sea water contains about 35 000 mg/dm3. How do these compare?

options.text: Sea water contains roughly three times as much
Sea water contains only about twice as much
The two values are of a similar order of magnitude
Sea water contains three orders of magnitude more

items.why: 35 000 divided by 12 is roughly 3000, which is a factor of about a thousand.

items.stem: Why is potable water not described as pure water in the chemical sense?

options.text: Because it still contains some dissolved substances
Because it has not been boiled before it is drunk
Because pure water simply means water that is clean and safe
Because a small number of microbes are always left in it

items.why: Potable water contains dissolved substances, so it is a mixture and not chemically pure.

items.stem: What does the specification say drinking water should have for humans?

options.text: No dissolved salts and no microbes whatsoever in it
Low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
Only water molecules, with everything else removed
Dissolved salts removed but microbes are left in

items.why: The specification states drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.

items.stem: Why do the methods used to produce potable water differ from one country to another?

options.text: Because the same standard process is used in every country
Because sea water is the cheapest source in every country
Because some sources already look clean enough to drink
Because they depend on available supplies and local conditions

items.why: The specification states that the methods depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.

items.stem: In the UK, what is the first step in producing most potable water?

options.text: Choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
Desalinating sea water taken from around the coast
Adding chlorine into the water at the source
Distilling sea water because supplies are unlimited

items.why: The specification lists choosing an appropriate source of fresh water as the first step.

items.stem: Why is water passed through filter beds during treatment?

options.text: To kill the microbes in the water before it is drunk
To remove the insoluble solids and large particles
To take the dissolved salts out of the water supply
To lower the pH of the water before it is stored

items.why: Filter beds physically remove insoluble solids and larger particles.

items.stem: What is achieved by the sterilising step in water treatment?

options.text: The grit and larger insoluble particles are taken out
The dissolved salts in the water are removed from it
Harmful microbes present in the water are killed
The water becomes chemically pure and contains only H2O

items.why: Sterilising kills microbes so that the water is safe to drink.

items.stem: Which set of sterilising agents for potable water is given in the specification?

options.text: Chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light are all used
Chlorine and ozone only, as light adds nothing
Sand, gravel and fine activated charcoal beds
Sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid

items.why: These are the three sterilising agents the specification names.

items.stem: Which two methods of desalination does the specification name?

options.text: Filtering through sand, then sterilising it with chlorine
Distillation, or a membrane process like reverse osmosis
Crystallisation of the salt, followed by sedimentation
Anaerobic digestion followed by aerobic treatment

items.why: The specification names distillation and processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis.

items.stem: The UK has plentiful rain. Why is desalination not used to supply most of its potable water?

options.text: Because sea water contains no dissolved salts in the UK
Because membranes cannot remove salt from sea water
Because desalination requires large amounts of energy
Because desalination is cheap but produces too little water

items.why: The specification states desalination requires large amounts of energy, and rain supplies the UK with fresh water.

items.stem: How does the treatment of salty water differ from the treatment of ground water?

options.text: Salty water is filtered while ground water is only sterilised
Ground water must be desalinated just like salty water
Both are treated in exactly the same way at the works
Salty water must have its dissolved salts removed

items.why: Ground water needs filtering and sterilising; salty water needs dissolved salts removed as well.

items.stem: In Required practical 8, how is the mass of dissolved solids in a water sample found?

options.text: By measuring the pH of the water sample with a probe
By evaporating a set volume to dryness and weighing the residue
By weighing the distillate collected during distillation
By filtering the sample and weighing the filter paper

items.why: The dissolved solids are left behind when the water evaporates, so the residue can be weighed.

items.stem: A student distils a sample of sea water in Required practical 8. What is collected in the receiving tube?

options.text: Salt solution that is more concentrated than before
Sea water with all of its dissolved solids in it
Water that leaves no residue when it is evaporated
Water that must be pure because its pH is 7

items.why: Only water evaporates and condenses, so the distillate is pure water and leaves no residue.

items.stem: Why may industrial waste water need treatment that sewage does not?

options.text: Because it is always released straight into the rivers
Because it contains no organic matter at all
Because only industrial waste contains harmful microbes
Because it may contain harmful chemicals as well

items.why: The specification says industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.

items.stem: What is the purpose of screening and grit removal at a sewage works?

options.text: To remove large solid objects and the grit
To kill the harmful microbes present in the sewage
To take the dissolved substances out of sewage
To digest the organic matter without any oxygen

items.why: Screening and grit removal takes out large solid objects and grit at the start of treatment.

items.stem: What two things does sedimentation produce during sewage treatment?

options.text: Solid effluent at the base and liquid sludge above
Microbes at the base and dissolved solids above
Sewage sludge, which settles, and effluent above it
Leachate solution and ash containing compounds

items.why: Sedimentation produces sewage sludge as the settled solid and effluent as the liquid.

items.stem: Which statement about the biological stages of sewage treatment is correct?

options.text: Sludge is treated aerobically and effluent anaerobically
The effluent from sedimentation is digested anaerobically
The microbes are removed when the sludge is screened
Sludge is digested anaerobically and effluent treated aerobically

items.why: The specification lists anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge and aerobic biological treatment of effluent.

items.stem: Rank waste water, ground water and salt water by how easily potable water is obtained from them, easiest first.

options.text: Ground water, then waste water, then salt water
Salt water first, then ground water, then waste water
Waste water, then salt water, and ground water last
All three of them are equally easy to treat

items.why: Ground water needs only filtering and sterilising; waste water needs more stages; salt water needs desalination.

items.stem: Why are new methods of extracting copper from low-grade ores being developed?

options.text: Because recycling means ore supplies can never run out
Because the copper ores left are becoming scarce
Because low-grade ores give the highest yields of metal
Because traditional mining cannot extract any copper

items.why: The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited and copper ores are becoming scarce.

items.stem: Which statement describes phytomining?

options.text: Bacteria break down the rock and leave copper metal behind
Plants absorb copper metal and store it in their leaves
Rock is dug up, moved and then disposed of in large heaps
The plants absorb metal compounds and are then burned to give ash

items.why: The specification states that plants absorb metal compounds, are harvested and burned to give ash containing metal compounds.

items.stem: What do the bacteria used in bioleaching produce?

options.text: Leachate solutions containing metal compounds
Pure copper metal that is left behind in the rock
Copper metal stored inside the plant leaves
A copper oxide gas released into the air

items.why: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.

items.stem: Scrap iron is added to a solution of a copper compound. What happens and why?

options.text: The copper displaces the iron because copper is more reactive
Iron displaces the copper because iron is more reactive
Nothing happens because the two metals are equally reactive
The iron is electrolysed at the positive electrode

items.why: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so iron displaces copper from the solution.

items.stem: A student compares phytomining with traditional mining of copper. Which comparison is valid?

options.text: Phytomining yields pure copper metal without further processing
Phytomining works best on the richest high-grade copper ores
Phytomining avoids moving large amounts of the rock
Phytomining removes the need to use any energy at all

items.why: The specification says these methods avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.

items.stem: The table shows water used per person per day: W 60 dm3, X 95 dm3, Y 180 dm3, Z 140 dm3. Which statement matches the table?

options.text: Country Y uses three times as much water per person as W
Country Y uses about twice as much per person as country W
Country Z uses more water per person than any other country
Country X uses the least water per person of the four

items.why: 180 divided by 60 is 3, so Y uses three times the volume W uses.

items.stem: A life cycle assessment is carried out on a new electric kettle. Which stages of the kettle's life does the assessment cover?

options.text: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, plus transport as a fifth
Manufacturing and packaging only, as that is where pollution comes from
Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacture, use, then disposal
Extraction, manufacture and use, but not disposal if it is recycled

items.why: These are the four stages named in the specification, with transport and distribution counted at each of them.

items.stem: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?

options.text: To assess the environmental impact of it across its whole life
To find the profit the product will make once it goes on sale
To measure the pollution given off by the factory that makes it
To produce one objective score that ranks it against rivals

items.why: This is the purpose given in the specification: to assess environmental impact in each of the four stages.

items.stem: An LCA is carried out on a poly(ethene) shopping bag. Which of these is counted in the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage?

options.text: Only the drilling for crude oil, and not the refining that follows it
Growing and harvesting the plants that most plastics are made from
Blowing molten polymer into a thin film to form the bag
Drilling for crude oil and processing it into poly(ethene)

items.why: The stage is 'extracting and processing raw materials', so the drilling and the processing into the polymer both belong to it.

items.stem: An LCA is carried out on a jar of jam sold in a glass jar. Which of these belongs to the 'manufacturing and packaging' stage?

options.text: Only the work done inside the factory, as transport is its own stage
Moulding the hot glass and boxing the jars for delivery
The cardboard tray is left out, as it is not part of the product
Quarrying the limestone and sand that the glass is made from

items.why: Shaping the product, and making and filling its packaging, are exactly what this stage covers.

items.stem: Two washing machines have the same impacts at every stage but one: machine A uses less electricity and less water per wash. Which stage of the LCA does this difference belong to?

options.text: Use and operation during its lifetime, as less energy and water are used
No stage at all, since electricity is used at home and not at a works
Manufacturing and packaging, since the factory sets how efficient it is
Disposal at the end of its useful life, as it will last a long time

items.why: Resources consumed while the machine is in service are counted in the third stage of the LCA.

items.stem: In an LCA of tinned food, where is the impact of the lorry journeys that carry the tins to the shops counted?

options.text: In a separate transport stage, added on after the four main stages
In manufacturing and packaging, as the factory arranges delivery
Nowhere, because the lorries belong to a delivery firm
Within each stage, since transport is included at all four stages

items.why: The specification includes transport and distribution at each stage, not as a stage of its own.

items.stem: A plastic garden chair is collected and buried in landfill at the end of its life. Which statement about the disposal stage of its LCA is correct?

options.text: Nothing is counted, because a chair sent to landfill is not processed
The transport of the chair and the burying of it are counted
Only the burying counts, since the lorry journey is a separate stage
Only the land the chair takes up in the landfill is counted

items.why: Disposal includes collection and transport as well as the landfill itself, since transport is counted at each stage.

items.stem: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?

options.text: The harm a pollutant does to a nearby river
How strongly local people object to the works
The mass of water used to make the item
The worth of the wildlife lost near a mine

items.why: Use of water is named in the specification as something that can be quantified fairly easily.

items.stem: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?

options.text: Because different scientists measure the energy used in different units
Because the mass of waste made can never be measured accurately
Because a shortened LCA was used, so it is only slightly less precise
Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements

items.why: This is the reason the specification gives for an LCA not being a purely objective process.

items.stem: Two teams carry out a full LCA on the same paint and reach opposite conclusions, although both used the same measured data for water, energy and waste. What is the best explanation?

options.text: One of the two teams must have made an arithmetic error somewhere
The teams gave the pollutant effects of this paint different weights
Pollutant effects cannot go into an LCA at all, so both teams guessed
Data on water and energy use is unreliable and varies by team

items.why: Allocating values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, so the same data can support different conclusions.

items.stem: What is the main risk of using a selective or abbreviated LCA?

options.text: It gives less accurate figures, as fewer decimal places are used
It removes all of the value judgements from the assessment
It can be used to support a conclusion decided beforehand
It takes much longer to carry out than a full study

items.why: The specification warns that selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.

items.stem: An advert calls a new drinks carton 'the greenest on the market', citing an LCA that assessed only the manufacturing stage. Which criticism of the claim is valid?

options.text: Stages that favour rival cartons have been left out
Advertising claims can never be based on data from an LCA
Manufacturing impacts cannot be quantified in a reliable way
Manufacturing is the only stage an LCA is able to assess

items.why: A selective LCA that omits extraction, use and disposal can be shaped to support a pre-determined conclusion.

items.stem: A comparative LCA of a plastic bag and a paper bag shows that the paper bag needs more energy and more water to make. A student concludes that paper bags are worse for the environment. Why is that conclusion unsafe?

options.text: Paper comes from trees, so a paper bag can have no impact at all
The remaining stages, including reuse and disposal, have not been considered
Energy and water use cannot be quantified, so the figures mean little
A shortened LCA like this is only a little less accurate

items.why: A comparative LCA must cover all four stages before either bag can be judged overall.

items.stem: In a comparative LCA of shopping bags, which factor has the greatest effect on the environmental impact per use of a bag?

options.text: Nothing after manufacture, as the impact is fixed at the factory
Whether the material will break down in a landfill site
The number of times the bag is reused before it is thrown out
Whether the bag is made of paper rather than plastic

items.why: The impact of making the bag is divided by the number of uses, so reuse lowers the impact per use.

items.stem: In a simple comparative LCA, why can a paper shopping bag have a greater impact than a plastic one at the raw materials and manufacturing stages?

options.text: More energy and water are needed to turn the wood into paper
Paper rots away, and biodegradable materials cost more to manufacture
Plastic bags come from a renewable source, but paper bags do not
Paper bags are heavier, so they take longer to rot down

items.why: Pulping and drying are energy and water intensive, and a paper bag needs far more material by mass.

items.stem: Which action by an end user reduces the use of limited resources by the greatest amount?

options.text: Recycling each product carefully after using it once
Choosing products whose packaging can be recycled
Recycling as much of the packaging as possible
Buying fewer new products in the first place

items.why: Reduction in use avoids extraction, manufacture, transport and disposal altogether, so it saves the most.

items.stem: Aluminium drinks cans are collected and recycled instead of being replaced by new aluminium extracted from its ore. Which statement about this is correct?

options.text: Recycling the cans needs no energy at all, unlike extraction
Aluminium ore becomes renewable once the cans are recycled
Less ore has to be mined and far less energy is needed overall
The recycled aluminium is purer than metal made from ore

items.why: Recycling reduces both the use of a limited raw material and the energy needed to obtain the metal.

items.stem: Which statement about the raw materials used to make metals, glass, clay ceramics and most plastics is correct?

options.text: Most plastics are made from plants, so they are a renewable source
They are unlimited, because these products can be recycled
Only metals are limited; glass and clay are unlimited
They all come from limited raw materials found in the Earth

items.why: The specification states that all of these are produced from limited raw materials.

items.stem: A company quarries limestone to make cement. Which of these is the best description of the environmental impact of the quarrying?

options.text: Dust, noise and the loss of habitat around the quarry site
There is no lasting impact, as the site will be landscaped later
The only impact is the fuel burned by the machines there
None, as limestone re-forms quickly and can be quarried again

items.why: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying causes exactly these local environmental impacts.

items.stem: A glass bottle is returned to the dairy, washed and then filled with milk again. Which term describes what has happened to the bottle, and why?

options.text: Recycling, because the glass has been used for a second time
Reuse, because the bottle is used again as it is
Reduction, because fewer new bottles now need making
Recycling, since the bottle was collected for processing

items.why: The object itself is used again without the material being reprocessed, which is reuse.

items.stem: Waste glass bottles are crushed and melted, and the glass is then made into new glass jars. Why is this recycling rather than reuse?

options.text: The glass has been reprocessed and made into a different product
It is reuse, because the same glass is being used once more
Recycled glass must always be turned back into bottles
It is reduction, because fewer new jars have to be made

items.why: Crushing and melting reprocesses the material, so the bottles have been recycled, not reused.

items.stem: How are metals recycled?

options.text: They are reused directly without any melting or processing
They are melted and then recast or reformed into products
They are melted only when every metal has been separated
They are crushed to powder and pressed into new shapes

items.why: This is the method given in the specification for recycling metals.

items.stem: At a steelworks, some scrap steel is added to the molten iron that comes from a blast furnace. Why is this done?

options.text: It acts as a fuel in the furnace, so less coke has to be burned
It removes the need to use any iron ore at the works at all
It separates unwanted metals out of the molten iron
It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from ore

items.why: This is the reason given in the specification: less iron then has to be extracted from iron ore.

items.stem: A council has data on four schemes. New raw material avoided each year: repair scheme 900 t, kerbside recycling 400 t, recycled bin bags 120 t, burning waste 0 t. Which scheme cuts the use of limited resources the most?

options.text: Kerbside recycling of bottles and cans
A repair scheme for household goods
Bin bags made from recycled waste
Burning waste to generate electricity

items.why: The data gives the repair scheme 900 t, the largest saving of new raw material.

items.stem: A plastic bag needs 0.6 MJ to make and is used once. A paper bag needs 2.0 MJ to make and is reused 4 times. What is the energy used per use of the paper bag?

options.text: 0.5 MJ
2.0 MJ
8.0 MJ
1.4 MJ

items.why: Impact per use is the total divided by the number of uses: 2.0 MJ divided by 4 is 0.5 MJ.

items.stem: A comparative LCA gives the energy to make each bag: paper 2.0 MJ, plastic 0.6 MJ. A shopper reuses a paper bag 10 times and uses a plastic bag once. Which conclusion do these figures support?

options.text: Per use the paper bag uses less energy than the plastic bag
The plastic bag uses less energy per use than the paper
Energy use cannot be quantified, so the figures prove nothing
Plastic comes from a renewable source, so plastic wins

items.why: 2.0 MJ shared over 10 uses is 0.2 MJ per use, which is below the plastic bag's 0.6 MJ.
